---
title: "Life Expectancy and National Income: Cross-Sectional and Within-Country Correlations"
subtitle: "An observational study reported following the STROBE guidelines"
---

<span class="kicker">Machine Learning for Social Science &nbsp;·&nbsp; Boston, MA</span>

::: {.lead}
This post treats a familiar relationship, life expectancy and income, as a small
observational study, reported in the structure epidemiologists use for
cross-sectional and cohort research (the STROBE guidelines). The question is
methodological: does a correlation observed **across countries at one point in
time** describe the same relationship as a correlation observed **within a
country over time**?
:::

## Abstract

**Design.** Observational correlational study with three components: a
cross-section of countries, a single-country time series, and within-country time
series for every country with sufficient data. **Objective.** To estimate and
compare the correlation between life expectancy and GDP per capita across
countries and within countries over time. **Methods.** Publicly available
national statistics; Pearson correlation coefficients on untransformed and
log-transformed income, and on year-over-year changes. **Results.** Across 175
countries in 2023&ndash;2024, r = 0.86 (log income; p = 8.6&times;10<sup>&minus;53</sup>).
Within the United States, 1960&ndash;2024, r = 0.97 (log income;
p = 2.5&times;10<sup>&minus;40</sup>). Across 203 countries, the median within-country
correlation was 0.87, but 19 countries had significant *negative* correlations,
several of them low-income countries where life expectancy rose by more than 20
years while GDP per capita fell. Correlations of year-over-year changes were close
to zero in most countries (median r = 0.10). **Conclusion.** The strong level
correlations largely reflect shared long-run trends. Large health gains occurred
in some countries without income growth, which is consistent with, but does not
establish, a role for health improvements that do not depend on GDP growth.

## Introduction

### Background and rationale

The association between national income and population health is one of the
best-documented regularities in economic demography. Preston (1975) showed that
across countries, life expectancy rises steeply with income at low incomes and
flattens at high incomes. That finding, the Preston curve, is **cross-sectional**:
different countries compared at one point in time.

Whether the same association holds **within** a country as it develops over time
is a separate question. A relationship that is strong across units need not
describe the path of any single unit, a problem known as the ecological fallacy
(Robinson, 1950). Preston himself found that the cross-sectional curve shifted
upward over the twentieth century, so that most of the gain in life expectancy
over that period could not be attributed to income growth along a fixed curve.

Correlation is the simplest tool for asking whether two variables move together,
and it can be applied in both dimensions: across units at a point in time, and
within a unit across time. This study applies the same statistic in both
dimensions to the same pair of variables, so that differences in the results can
be attributed to the design rather than to the method.

### Objectives

1. To estimate the correlation between life expectancy and GDP per capita across
   countries at one point in time (cross-sectional design).
2. To estimate the same correlation within the United States over 65 years
   (single-country time-series design).
3. To estimate the within-country time-series correlation for every country with
   sufficient data, and to describe how it varies across countries and regions.
4. To consider what a correlation coefficient can and cannot establish in each
   design.

## Methods

### Study design

Three designs are reported. (i) **Cross-section:** each country contributes one
observation at approximately the same point in time. (ii) **Single-country time
series:** the United States contributes one observation per year from 1960 to
2024. (iii) **Multi-country time series:** for each country, a separate
correlation is computed across that country's own years, producing one
correlation coefficient per country. All designs are purely observational.

### Setting

The cross-section uses the most recent year available in each source (GDP per
capita: 2023; life expectancy: most recent CIA World Factbook estimate, referenced
2024). Both time-series designs cover 1960 to 2024, the full span of the World
Development Indicators (WDI) series.

### Participants (units of analysis)

**Cross-section:** all countries and territories with both a life expectancy and a
GDP per capita value in the sources below, matched by name with manual
reconciliation of naming differences. Of 229 countries and territories with a life
expectancy estimate, 175 (76%) had a matching GDP figure and were included.

**United States time series:** all 65 years from 1960 to 2024; none missing.

**Multi-country time series:** all World Bank economies in the WDI files, excluding
regional and income-group aggregates, with at least 20 years in which both series
were reported. 203 economies met this criterion. The median number of years per
country was 65 (range 20&ndash;65). Countries were grouped by the World Bank region
listed in the WDI country metadata, used as published (which places Afghanistan,
Pakistan and Malta in Middle East &amp; North Africa, and Greenland in Europe &amp;
Central Asia).

### Variables

**Outcome:** life expectancy at birth, in years: the average number of years a
newborn would live if the age-specific mortality rates of that year persisted
throughout its life.

**Exposure:** GDP per capita. In the cross-section, current US dollars. In both
time-series designs, constant 2015 US dollars, which removes inflation so that
changes over time reflect real income.

### Data sources and measurement

| Cross-section | GDP per capita, 2023 (current US dollars) | World Bank Open Data, via Lumistats | <https://lumistats.com/rankings/gdp/> |
| US time series | Life expectancy, 1960&ndash;2024 | World Bank WDI, series SP.DYN.LE00.IN, via FRED (series SPDYNLE00INUSA) | <https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/SPDYNLE00INUSA> |
| US time series | GDP per capita, 1960&ndash;2024 (constant 2015 US dollars) | World Bank WDI, series NY.GDP.PCAP.KD, via FRED (series NYGDPPCAPKDUSA) | <https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/NYGDPPCAPKDUSA> |
| Multi-country time series | Life expectancy at birth, total (years), 1960&ndash;2024 | World Bank WDI, SP.DYN.LE00.IN (last updated 13 July 2026) | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.LE00.IN> |
| Multi-country time series | GDP per capita (constant 2015 US dollars), 1960&ndash;2024 | World Bank WDI, NY.GDP.PCAP.KD (last updated 13 July 2026) | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD> |
| Multi-country time series | Region classification | WDI country metadata files distributed with the two series above | (as above) |

### Bias

Four sources of bias are noted. First, the cross-section combines life expectancy
and GDP from different producers and reference years. Second, WDI life expectancy
for many low- and middle-income countries is modeled by the UN Population Division
rather than measured annually from vital registration; modeled series are smooth,
which mechanically weakens correlations of year-over-year changes. Third, no
adjustment was made for variables that affect both income and health (education,
disease environment, conflict, governance). Fourth, in the time-series designs,
calendar time itself is a common driver: medical and public health technology
improved throughout the period regardless of any one country's income.

### Study size

Study size was determined by data availability: 175 countries in the
cross-section, 65 years for the United States, and 203 countries (median 65 years
each) in the multi-country time series. No power calculation was performed.

### Quantitative variables

GDP per capita was analyzed untransformed and natural-log transformed. The log
transform was included because the relationship is known to be concave, and a
Pearson correlation on untransformed income understates a strong but curved
association. Life expectancy was analyzed in years.

### Statistical methods

All associations are Pearson product-moment correlation coefficients. The formula
is the same in every design; only the index changes.

**Cross-section**, across countries *i* = 1, &hellip;, *n*:

$$
r_{\text{CS}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar{y})^2}}
$$

**Time series** for country *c*, across years *t* = 1, &hellip;, *T*<sub>c</sub>:

$$
r_{c} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T_c}(x_{ct}-\bar{x}_c)(y_{ct}-\bar{y}_c)}{\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T_c}(x_{ct}-\bar{x}_c)^2\;\sum_{t=1}^{T_c}(y_{ct}-\bar{y}_c)^2}}
$$

where *x* is GDP per capita (or its natural log) and *y* is life expectancy.

**Significance.** Each coefficient is tested against the null hypothesis of no
correlation using

$$
t = r\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}}, \qquad p = 2\,\Pr\left(T_{n-2} > |t|\right),
$$

with *n* the number of countries (cross-section) or years (time series). Because
*t* grows with both *r* and *n*, strong correlations in long series produce
extremely small p-values. The test assumes independent observations.

**Year-over-year changes.** To separate co-movement from shared trends, the
within-country correlation was also computed on annual changes, using consecutive
years only:

$$
\Delta y_{ct} = y_{ct} - y_{c,t-1}, \qquad \Delta x_{ct} = \ln X_{ct} - \ln X_{c,t-1},
$$

where Δ*x* is approximately the annual growth rate of GDP per capita. If life
expectancy and income are linked year to year, Δ*x* and Δ*y* should be
correlated. If they merely trend together over decades, the level correlation
will be high while the change correlation is near zero.

No regression model was fit. This choice is deliberate and is returned to in the
Conclusion.

**When a correlation is a valid tool, and when it is not.** A Pearson correlation
validly summarizes the strength and direction of a linear (or, after
transformation, monotonic) association, and its significance test is valid when
observations are independent. It becomes an unreliable guide to the underlying
relationship in three situations relevant here. First, when a **third variable**
moves both *x* and *y* (confounding). Second, when the data are **aggregates**: a
correlation across country averages can differ in sign or size from the
correlation within any country, and vice versa (the ecological fallacy). Third,
in time series, when both variables share a **common trend**: two unrelated series
that both rise for decades will correlate strongly, with time as the omitted
third variable (Yule, 1926; Granger and Newbold, 1974). In that case consecutive
observations are also strongly autocorrelated, so the effective sample size is
far smaller than the number of years and the p-values above are too small.

**Why life expectancy and GDP per capita are a good test case.** The relationship
is real, large and well replicated, with plausible mechanisms (income buys
nutrition, sanitation and medical care), so it is not a trivial example. It also
displays all three pitfalls: income is correlated with many confounders across
countries; the cross-sectional curve is known to have shifted over time; and life
expectancy rose almost everywhere after 1960 through medical and public health
advances that were partly independent of national income.

## Results

### Participants

The cross-section included 175 of 229 countries and territories (76%). The US
time series included all 65 years. The multi-country analysis included 203
economies; 105 contributed all 65 years.

### Descriptive statistics

::: {style="overflow-x:auto;"}

| Design | Variable | n | Mean | Median | SD | Min | Max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cross-section (countries, 2023&ndash;24) | Life expectancy (years) | 175 | 74.4 | 75.6 | 7.0 | 54.4 | 89.8 |
| Cross-section (countries, 2023&ndash;24) | GDP per capita (current US dollars) | 175 | 20,883 | 7,133 | 33,282 | 251 | 256,800 |
| Time series (US, 1960&ndash;2024) | Life expectancy (years) | 65 | 75.0 | 75.4 | 3.0 | 69.8 | 78.9 |
| Time series (US, 1960&ndash;2024) | GDP per capita (constant 2015 US dollars) | 65 | 40,950 | 39,448 | 13,780 | 18,992 | 66,857 |

:::

The cross-sectional GDP distribution is heavily right-skewed (mean almost three
times the median). The US series is close to symmetric over its narrower
3.5-fold range. Descriptive statistics for each of the 203 countries are in
Appendix A.

Both designs show a strong positive correlation in levels, stronger with log
income, as expected for a concave relationship. In the United States, however, the
correlation of annual changes is essentially zero: years of faster income growth
were not years of faster gains in life expectancy.

**Levels.** Most countries look like the United States. The median within-country
correlation was 0.87, and 168 of 203 countries (83%) had a significant positive
correlation. But the United States is not typical of the whole distribution: 48
countries had a correlation below 0.5, 27 had a negative correlation, and 19 of
those were significantly negative. Correlations were weakest in Sub-Saharan
Africa (median 0.55, with 9 countries not significant and 5 significantly
negative) and strongest in Europe &amp; Central Asia, North America and South Asia
(medians of 0.93 or above).

The significantly negative countries fall into three groups. The first is
low-income countries where GDP per capita stagnated or fell for decades,
including Madagascar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, Liberia, Niger
and Burundi. The second is oil-rich economies whose GDP per capita declined from
very high levels as populations grew and oil revenues fell, including Brunei, the
United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, along with Venezuela. The third is
small, high-income island territories such as Curaçao, French Polynesia, Nauru,
the US Virgin Islands and the Northern Mariana Islands. In every group, life
expectancy rose while income did not, so the two trends ran in opposite
directions.

**Table 3.** Selected countries: change in life expectancy and GDP per capita over
the observation period, with the United States for comparison.

::: {style="overflow-x:auto;"}

| Country | Period | Life expectancy (years) | GDP per capita (constant 2015 US dollars) | r (levels, ln GDP) | r (changes) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liberia | 1960&ndash;2024 | 38.1 &rarr; 62.3 (+24.3) | 2,444 &rarr; 665 (&minus;73%) | &minus;0.63 | 0.59 |
| Niger | 1960&ndash;2024 | 36.2 &rarr; 61.4 (+25.2) | 742 &rarr; 589 (&minus;21%) | &minus;0.59 | 0.13 |
| Congo, Dem. Rep. | 1960&ndash;2024 | 40.8 &rarr; 62.1 (+21.3) | 1,303 &rarr; 554 (&minus;57%) | &minus;0.81 | 0.14 |
| Haiti | 1960&ndash;2024 | 43.4 &rarr; 65.1 (+21.7) | 1,735 &rarr; 1,155 (&minus;33%) | &minus;0.69 | 0.26 |
| Madagascar | 1960&ndash;2024 | 43.3 &rarr; 63.8 (+20.5) | 812 &rarr; 454 (&minus;44%) | &minus;0.88 | 0.28 |
| Burundi | 1960&ndash;2024 | 43.3 &rarr; 63.8 (+20.6) | 252 &rarr; 269 (+6%) | &minus;0.36 | 0.15 |
| United States | 1960&ndash;2024 | 69.8 &rarr; 78.9 (+9.1) | 18,992 &rarr; 66,857 (+252%) | 0.97 | &minus;0.03 |

:::

In these low-income countries life expectancy rose by roughly 20 to 25 years,
about two to three times the US gain, while real GDP per capita fell by between a
fifth and nearly three quarters (Burundi was roughly flat).

**Year-over-year changes.** Once trends are removed, the correlation largely
disappears. The median correlation of annual changes was 0.10. Only 44 countries
(22%) showed a significant positive correlation and 4 a significant negative
one; the remaining 155 (76%) were not significant. The largest positive change
correlations occurred in countries with episodes in which a crisis hit income and
mortality in the same years, such as Rwanda (r = 0.86) and Liberia (r = 0.59).
Notably, several countries with negative level correlations have positive change
correlations: a war or collapse lowers both income and life expectancy at the same
time, even though over the longer run the two trends diverge.

## Discussion

### Key results

The cross-section and the US time series both show a strong positive
correlation in levels. Extending the time-series design to 203 countries shows
that the US result is common but not universal: about one in four countries has a
level correlation below 0.5, and 19 have significant negative correlations. In
nearly all countries, the correlation of year-over-year changes is close to zero.

### Can health improve without income growth?

The countries in Table 3 are the most direct evidence in this study on that
question. Liberia, Niger, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti and
Madagascar each gained more than 20 years of life expectancy over a period in
which their real GDP per capita fell. Whatever drove those gains, it was not
domestic income growth. This is consistent with a long literature arguing that
mortality can fall substantially at low income: Caldwell (1986) on "routes to low
mortality in poor countries," Riley (2008) on low-income countries with high
longevity, and Cutler, Deaton and Lleras-Muney (2006), who argue that the spread
of knowledge and technology, such as vaccination, oral rehydration, antibiotics
and malaria control, explains more of the mortality decline than income does.
Much of this was delivered through public programs and international health
financing rather than private spending, which points toward a policy case that
health investment need not wait for growth.

Four cautions apply before drawing that conclusion from these data:

- **The counterfactual is unknown.** A correlation cannot say whether these
  countries would have gained even more with income growth. Gains without growth
  are not evidence that growth does not matter.
- **The drivers are not measured here.** No policy variable was observed. The
  pattern is consistent with health policy, imported medical technology, external
  aid and falling fertility, but this study does not distinguish among them.
- **Not all negative correlations reflect health policy.** In the oil economies
  and small island territories, GDP per capita fell from already high levels while
  life expectancy continued to rise. These cases reflect commodity prices and
  population growth rather than health gains achieved in poverty.
- **Measurement.** Life expectancy in many low-income countries is modeled rather
  than measured each year, which makes the series smoother than the underlying
  reality.

The appropriate conclusion is that the data are consistent with large health
gains without income growth, and that this hypothesis merits a design that can
test it: for example, relating within-country changes in life expectancy to
measured health interventions such as vaccination coverage or public health
spending.

### Limitations

This is a correlational analysis of unadjusted, aggregated national statistics.
No confounders were controlled for. In both time-series designs the level
correlations are dominated by shared trends, and because consecutive years are
strongly autocorrelated, the reported level p-values overstate statistical
significance; the effective number of independent observations is far smaller
than the number of years. The cross-section combines two data producers and two
reference years. Finally, a single Pearson r reports the strength of an
association but not its slope, so it cannot show whether the cross-sectional and
within-country relationships have the same shape.

### Interpretation

Life expectancy and income are strongly correlated across countries and, in
levels, within most countries over time. The within-country level correlation
mainly reflects the fact that life expectancy rose almost everywhere after 1960:
where income also rose, the correlation is strongly positive; where income fell,
it is strongly negative; and year-to-year changes are only weakly related in
either case. A correlation coefficient cannot distinguish a direct effect of
income from a common trend, and the multi-country results suggest the common
trend accounts for much of what the single-country US correlation appears to
show.

### Generalizability

The cross-sectional estimate describes the 175 included countries at one point in
time and should not be read as describing the path of any single country. The US
time series describes the United States only. The multi-country results show
directly that within-country relationships vary widely, and that the United States
is an example of the most common pattern rather than a representative case.

## Conclusion and next steps

All three designs return strong correlations in levels, but the multi-country
analysis shows that the within-country correlation can be strong and positive,
near zero, or strong and negative, and that it largely disappears in
year-over-year changes. The next post in this series will fit unadjusted ordinary
least squares (OLS) regressions to the same data. That adds what a correlation
cannot provide: an explicit slope (years of life expectancy per unit of log
income) that can be compared directly between the cross-section and the
within-country series; an R&sup2; for each design; and residual plots showing where
countries depart from the fitted relationship. Regression will remain unadjusted
for confounders, and the trend problem identified here will carry over to it,
which motivates later steps such as models in differences and models with
country and year effects.
